title: Destination-aware pseudonymization and retention routing for telemetry exports
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Context:
Redwood Console emits rich telemetry (route metrics, token-level cost breakdowns, user interactions) that currently flows to multiple downstream destinations: internal analytics, long-term audit store, third-party observability, and partner exports. Each destination has different PII and retention requirements (e.g., internal analytics: 90 days with pseudonymized user ids; audit store: 7 years with full traceability for enterprise customers; partner exports: per-customer contract TTLs and per-field suppression).

Problem:
We lack a single routing layer that (a) applies destination-specific pseudonymization or redaction policies, (b) attaches and enforces per-destination retention TTLs, and (c) records an auditable transformation manifest for compliance. Current ad-hoc scrubbing is duplicated in multiple services and causes divergence, unexpected PII leakage (a recent near-miss in a partner export), and expensive backfills when policies change.

Goal:
Build a destination-aware scrubbing & routing proxy in the Console ingestion path that:
1) Applies schema-aware pseudonymization or redaction rules per destination (column-level)
2) Emits a cryptographic transformation manifest (hash anchors + policy version) for each event for downstream verification and auditability
3) Enforces per-destination retention TTLs and materializes deletion manifests for downstream sinks
4) Provides a migration path for existing consumers with zero- or low-downtime cutover

Acceptance criteria:
- New proxy can route events to at least three destinations with distinct policies configured (internal analytics, audit-store, partner-export).
- Column-level policies implemented for: user_id (pseudonymize with salted HMAC), email (hash + redact if partner policy disallows), full_text (regex-based redaction with whitelist exceptions).
- A transformation manifest is produced and stored in S3 (or object store) with SHA256 anchor, policy version, and event id; manifests are queryable via the Console privacy audit UI.
- Downstream retention enforcement: when TTL expires the proxy emits deletion-manifests and marks manifests as revoked; a downstream consumer test confirms the record is removed from internal analytics after simulated TTL.
- Migration: can opt a single destination to use the proxy and validate parity against legacy path for 7 days with sampled comparison metrics showing <=0.01% dropped fields and no PII regressions.

Design notes / tradeoffs:
- We chose an in-path proxy (sidecar service in ingestion fleet) rather than a central post-processor to reduce duplicated network hops and keep per-event policy decision latency <5ms p50. This increases coupling with ingestion traffic and requires strong autoscaling.
- Pseudonymization strategy: salted HMAC per-customer + key rotation afford unlinkability across rotations if required. We considered irreversible tokenization vs reversible encryption; reversible encryption would help debug but increases risk surface and KMS obligations. For compliance requests reversible paths will be handled via the existing erasure workflow rather than adding decryption into the proxy.
- Transformation manifests are intentionally minimal (hash anchors + metadata) to avoid storing raw PII; we do not store plaintext in S3. The anchor allows downstream verification that a particular event variant was delivered under policy X.
- Policy config will be expressed in a declarative YAML + schema descriptors. Policy evaluation will be schema-aware (using the console event schema registry) to avoid mistaken redactions of nested fields.

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 1 (spike, 2w): implement prototype proxy that performs user_id HMAC and routes to two mock sinks; measure latency and throughput. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/console-telemetry/pull/214 (prototype PR).
- Phase 2 (core, 3w): full policy engine (YAML-driven), manifest generation, S3 manifest writer, unit/integration tests. Add auth to manifest endpoint.
- Phase 3 (canary, 2w): wire up to real internal analytics and audit-store with opt-in sample rate (1%). Run parity checks and dashboards.
- Phase 4 (rollout, 2w): enable for partner-export destinations and implement deletion-manifest emitter and downstream contract tests.

Operational considerations:
- Autoscaling: proxy must scale to peak ingress (current peak 8k eps). We'll provision an HPA with custom metrics (incoming rps and queue length) and pre-warming for known spikes.
- Observability: add metrics for policy-evaluation-time, per-destination drop counts, manifest write success, and a PII-regression gauge.
- Backpressure: if manifest writer is degraded, proxy defaults to buffering with bounded queue and emits a backpressure metric; we will fail closed for partner exports (block) and fail open for internal analytics (to preserve business continuity) — this divergence is explicit in policy.

APIs & Config:
- /policy/v1/lookup?schema=console:event:route&version=2026-02 returns per-destination policy bundles.
- /proxy/v1/ingest accepts incoming events and returns {event_id, manifest_anchor}.

QA & test plan:
- Unit tests for each policy rule: pseudonymization, regex redaction, allowlist exceptions.
- Integration: sample-based parity test comparing legacy path to proxy for 1M events; automated diff tooling at https://github.com/redwood-inference/console-telemetry/tree/main/tools/parity.
- Compliance: run simulated deletion where TTL=1h and verify downstream deletion within SLA in test cluster.

Rollout plan:
1) Deploy proxy in staging and run full parity test.
2) Canary to 1% traffic for internal analytics; monitor PII-regression gauge and dropped-field rate.
3) Increase to 25% after 72h stable, then 100% for internal analytics.
4) Add audit-store canary and partner exports sequentially.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How will policy versioning interact with long-term audit retention (audit-store wants original policy id attached)? Proposed: manifest includes policy_version field and immutable policy artifacts archived in S3.
- Legal: confirm partner contract language allows pseudonymization vs full redaction for specific partners. Assigned to legal: @Nora Patel.
- Key rotation cadence: suggest quarterly; security to sign-off.
